{{Short description|Concept in dynamical systems}}
{{more citations needed|date=December 2018}}

In [[mathematics]], more specifically in [[dynamical system]]s, the '''method of averaging''' (also called averaging theory) exploits systems containing time-scales separation: a ''fast oscillation'' '''versus''' a ''slow drift''. It suggests that we perform an averaging over a given amount of time in order to iron out the fast oscillations and observe the qualitative behavior from the resulting dynamics. The approximated solution holds under finite time inversely proportional to the parameter denoting the slow time scale. It turns out to be a customary problem where there exists the trade off between how good is the approximated solution balanced by how much time it holds to be close to the original solution.

More precisely, the system has the following form
<math display="block"> \dot{x} = \varepsilon f( x,t , \varepsilon ), \quad 0 \leq \varepsilon \ll 1</math>of a phase space variable <math>x.</math>The ''fast oscillation'' is given by <math>f</math> '''versus''' a ''slow drift'' of  <math>\dot{x}</math>. The averaging method yields an autonomous dynamical system
<math display="block"> \dot{y}= \varepsilon {\frac {1}{T}}\int _{0}^{T}f(y, s, 0)~ds =: \varepsilon {\bar {f}}(y)</math>
which approximates the solution curves of <math>\dot{x}</math> inside a connected and compact region of the phase space and over time of <math>1/\varepsilon</math>.

Under the validity of this averaging technique, the asymptotic behavior of the original system is captured by the dynamical equation for <math>y</math>. In this way, qualitative methods for autonomous dynamical systems may be employed to analyze the [[equilibrium point|equilibria]] and more complex structures, such as [[slow manifold]] and [[invariant manifold]]s, as well as their [[Stability theory|stability]] in the phase space of the averaged system.

In addition, in a physical application it might be reasonable or natural to replace a mathematical model, which is given in the form of the differential equation for <math>\dot{x} </math>, with the corresponding averaged system <math>\dot{y}</math>, in order to use the averaged system to make a prediction and then test the prediction against the results of a physical experiment.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Ordinary differential equations with applications|last=Charles.|first=Chicone, Carmen|date=2006|publisher=Springer|isbn=9780387307695|edition=  2nd|location=New York|oclc=288193020}}</ref>

The averaging method has a long history, which is deeply rooted in [[Perturbation theory|perturbation]] problems that arose in [[celestial mechanics]] (see, for example in <ref name=":0">{{Cite book|date=2007|title=Averaging Methods in Nonlinear Dynamical Systems|volume=59|language=en-gb|doi=10.1007/978-0-387-48918-6| isbn=978-0-387-48916-2| last1=Sanders|first1=Jan A.|last2=Verhulst|first2=Ferdinand|last3=Murdock|first3=James|series=Applied Mathematical Sciences }}</ref>).

== First example ==
[[File:Logistic growth equation.png|thumb|403x403px|Figure 1: Solution to perturbed logistic growth equation <math>\dot {x} = \varepsilon (x (1 - x) + \sin{t}) ~ x \in \R, ~\varepsilon = 0.05</math> (blue solid line) and the averaged equation <math>\dot {y} = \varepsilon y (1 - y),~ y \in \R</math>  (orange solid line).]]
Consider a perturbed [[Logistic differential equation|logistic growth]]
<math display="block"> \dot {x} = \varepsilon (x (1 - x) + \sin{t}) \quad \quad x \in \R, \quad 0 \leq \varepsilon \ll 1,</math>
and the averaged equation
<math display="block"> \dot {y} = \varepsilon y (1 - y) \qquad y \in \R. </math>The purpose of the method of averaging is to tell us the qualitative behavior of the [[vector field]] when we average it over a period of time. It guarantees that the solution <math>y(t)</math> approximates <math>x(t)</math> for times <math>t = \mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon).</math> '''Exceptionally:''' in this example the approximation is even better, it is valid for all times. We present it in a section below.

== Definitions ==
We assume the vector field <math>f:\R^n \times \R \times \R \to \R^n</math> to be of [[differentiability class]] <math>C^{r}</math> with <math>r \geq 2</math> (or even we will only say smooth), which we will denote <math>f \in C^r(\R^n \times \R \times \R^+; \R^n)</math>.  We expand this time-dependent vector field in a [[Taylor series]] (in powers of <math>\varepsilon</math>) with remainder <math>f^{[k + 1]}(x, t, \varepsilon)</math>. We introduce the following notation:<ref name=":0" />
<math display="block"> f(x, t, \varepsilon) = f^0(x, t) + \varepsilon f^{1}(x, t) + \dots + \varepsilon^k f^{k}(x, t) + \varepsilon^{k + 1} f^{[k + 1]}(x, t, \varepsilon),</math>
where <math>f^{j} = \frac{f^{(j)}(x, t, 0)}{j!} </math>is the <math>j</math>-th derivative with <math>0 \leq j \leq k</math>. As we are concerned with averaging problems, in general <math>f^0(x, t)</math> is zero, so it turns out that we will be interested in vector fields given by
<math display="block"> f(x, t, \varepsilon) = \varepsilon f^{[1]}(x, t, \varepsilon) =  \varepsilon f^{1}(x, t) + \varepsilon^{2} f^{[2]}(x, t, \varepsilon).</math>
Besides, we define the following [[initial value problem]] to be in the '''standard form''':<ref name=":0" />
<math display="block">\dot{x} = \varepsilon f^{1}(x, t) + \varepsilon^{2} f^{[2]}(x, t, \varepsilon), \qquad x(0, \varepsilon) =: x_0 \in D \subseteq \R^n, \quad 0 \leq \varepsilon \ll 1.</math>

== Theorem: averaging in the periodic case ==
Consider for every <math>D \subset \R^n</math> connected and bounded  and every <math>\varepsilon_0 > 0</math> there exist <math>L > 0</math> and <math>\varepsilon \leq \varepsilon_0</math> such that the original system (a non-autonomous dynamical system) given by
<math display="block">\dot{x} = \varepsilon f^{1}(x, t) + \varepsilon^{2} f^{[2]}(x, t, \varepsilon), \qquad x_0 \in D \subseteq \R^n, \quad 0 \leq \varepsilon \ll 1,</math>
has solution <math>x(t, \varepsilon)</math>, where <math>f^1 \in C^r(D \times \R; \R^n)</math> is [[Frequency|periodic]] with period <math>T</math> and <math>f^{[2]} \in C^r(D \times \R \times  \R^+; \R^n)</math> both with <math>r \geq 2</math> bounded on bounded sets. Then there exists a constant <math>c > 0</math> such that the solution <math>y(t, \varepsilon)</math> of the ''averaged'' ''system''  (autonomous dynamical system) is
<math display="block"> \dot{y}= \varepsilon {\frac {1}{T}} \int _{0}^{T}f^1(y, s)~ds =: \varepsilon{\bar {f}}^1(y), \quad y(0, \varepsilon) = x_0</math>
is
<math display="block"> \|x(t, \varepsilon) - y(t, \varepsilon)\| < c \varepsilon</math>for <math>0 \leq \varepsilon \leq \varepsilon_0</math> and <math>0 \leq t \leq L/\varepsilon</math>.

=== Remarks ===

* There are two approximations in this what is called ''first approximation'' estimate: reduction to the average of the vector field and negligence of <math>\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)</math> terms. 
* Uniformity with respect to the initial condition <math>x_0</math>: if we vary <math>x_0</math> this affects the estimation of <math>L </math> and <math>c </math>. The proof and discussion of this can be found in J. Murdock's book.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Perturbations : theory and methods|last=Murdock|first= James A.|date=1999|publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics| isbn=978-0898714432| location=Philadelphia| oclc=41612407}}</ref>
* Reduction of regularity: there is a more general form of this theorem which requires only <math>f^1</math> to be [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz]] and <math>f^{[2]}</math> continuous. It is a more recent proof and can be seen in Sanders ''et al.''.<ref name=":0" /> The theorem statement presented here is due to the proof framework proposed by [[Krylov–Bogoliubov averaging method|Krylov-Bogoliubov]] which is based on an introduction of a near-identity transformation. The advantage of this method is the extension to more general settings such as infinite-dimensional systems - [[partial differential equation]] or delay differential equations.
*J. Hale presents generalizations to almost periodic vector-fields.<ref>{{Cite book | title=Ordinary differential equations| last=Hale | first = Jack K.| date=1980| publisher=R.E. Krieger Pub. Co| isbn=978-0898740110| edition= 2nd| location=Huntington, N.Y.| oclc=5170595}}</ref>

=== Strategy of the proof ===
[[Krylov–Bogoliubov averaging method|Krylov-Bogoliubov]] realized that the slow dynamics of the system determines the leading order of the asymptotic solution.

In order to prove it, they proposed a ''near-identity transformation,'' which turned out to be a change of coordinates with its own time-scale transforming the original system to the averaged one.

==== Sketch of the proof ====

# Determination of a near-identity transformation: the smooth mapping <math>y \mapsto U(y, t, \varepsilon) = y + \varepsilon u^{[1]}(y, t, \varepsilon)</math>where <math>u^{[1]} </math> is assumed to be regular enough and <math>T</math> periodic. The proposed change of coordinates is given by <math>x = U(y, t, \varepsilon)</math>. 
# Choose an appropriate <math>u^{[1]} </math>solving the '''homological equation''' of the averaging theory: <math>\frac{\partial u^{[1]}}{\partial t} = f^{1}(y, t) - \bar{f}^1(y)</math>. 
#Change of coordinates carries the original system to <math>\dot{y} = \varepsilon \bar{f}^1(y) + \varepsilon^2 f_{*}^{[2]}(y, t, \varepsilon).</math>
# Estimation of error due to truncation and comparison to the original variable.

== Non-autonomous class of systems: more examples ==
Along the history of the averaging technique, there is class of system extensively studied which give us meaningful examples we will discuss below. The class of system is given by:
<math display="block">\ddot{z} + z = \varepsilon g(z, \dot{z}, t), \qquad z \in \R,\quad  z(0) = z_0 ~\mathrm{ and }~ \dot{z}(0) = v_0,</math>
where <math>g</math> is smooth. This system is similar to a linear system with a small nonlinear perturbation given by 
<math>\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \varepsilon ~g(z, \dot{z}, t)  \end{bmatrix}</math>:
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\dot{z_1} &=  z_2, & z_1(0) &= z_0 \\
\dot{z_2} &= -z_1 + \varepsilon g(z_1, z_2, t), & z_2(0) &= v_0,
\end{aligned}</math>
differing from the standard form. Hence there is a necessity to perform a transformation to make it in the standard form explicitly.<ref name=":0" /> We are able to change coordinates using [[Variation of parameters|variation of constants]] method. We look at the unperturbed system, i.e. <math>\varepsilon = 0</math>, given by
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix} \dot{z_1} \\ \dot{z_2} \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} z_1 \\ z_2 \end{bmatrix}
= A \begin{bmatrix} z_1 \\ z_2 \end{bmatrix}
</math>

which has the [[fundamental solution]] <math>\Phi(t) = e^{A t}</math>corresponding to a rotation. Then the time-dependent change of coordinates is <math>z(t) = \Phi(t) x</math> where <math>x</math> is the coordinates respective to the standard form.

If we take the [[time derivative]] in both sides and invert the fundamental matrix we obtain
<math display="block"> \dot{x} = \varepsilon e^{- A t} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ ~\tilde g(x, \dot{x}, t)  \end{bmatrix} ~\text{ with }~ \tilde g(x, \dot{x}, t)=g(\cos(t)x(t)+\sin(t)\dot x(t), -\sin(t)x(t)+\cos(t)\dot x(t), t).</math>

=== Remarks ===

* The same can be done to time-dependent linear parts. Although the fundamental solution may be non-trivial to write down explicitly, the procedure is similar. See Sanders ''et al.'' <ref name=":0" /> for further details.
* If the eigenvalues of <math>A</math> are not all purely imaginary this is called [[Hyperbolic set|hyperbolicity condition]]. For this occasion, the perturbation equation may present some serious problems even whether <math>g</math> is bounded, since the solution grows exponentially fast.<ref name=":0" /> However, qualitatively, we may be able to know the asymptotic solution, such as [[Hartman–Grobman theorem|Hartman-Grobman]] results and more.<ref name=":1" />
* Occasionally, polar coordinates may yield standard forms that are simpler to analyze. Consider <math>z_1 = r \sin(t - \phi) ~\text{and}~ z_2 = r \cos(t - \phi) </math>, which determines the initial condition <math>(r(0), \phi(0)) </math> and the system <math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix} \dot{r} \\ \dot{\phi} \end{bmatrix} = \varepsilon
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(t - \phi) g(r \sin(t - \phi), r \cos(t - \phi), t) \\
\frac{1}{r} \sin(t - \phi) g(r \sin(t - \phi), r \cos(t - \phi), t)
\end{bmatrix}.</math>
If <math>g \in C^1</math>we may apply averaging so long as a neighborhood of the origin is excluded (since the polar coordinates fail):
<math display="block"> \begin{array}{rcl}
\bar{f}_1^1(r) & = & \displaystyle \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} \cos(s - \phi) g(r \sin (s - \phi), r \cos(s - \phi), s) ds \\[4pt]
\bar{f}_2^1(r) & = & \displaystyle \frac{1}{2 \pi r} \int_0^{2 \pi} \sin(s - \phi) g(r \sin (s - \phi), r \cos(s - \phi), s) ds,
\end{array}</math>
where the averaged system is
<math display="block"> \begin{array}{lcr}
\dot{\bar{r}} = \varepsilon \bar{f}_1^1 (\bar{r}) \\
\dot{\bar{\phi}} = \varepsilon \bar{f}_2^1 (\bar{r}).
\end{array}</math>

=== Example: Misleading averaging results ===
[[File:Averaging example Crude averaging z axis.png|alt=|thumb|610x610px|Figure 2: A simple harmonic oscillator with small periodic damping term given by <math>\ddot{z} + 4 \varepsilon \cos^2{(t)} \dot{z} + z = 0, ~  z(0) = 0,~ \dot{z}(0) = 1;~\varepsilon = 0.05</math>.The numerical simulation of the original equation (blue solid line) is compared with averaging system (orange dashed line) and the crude averaged system (green dash-dotted line). The left plot displays the solution evolved in time and the right plot represents on the phase space.  We note that the crude averaging disagrees with the expected solution.]]
The method contains some assumptions and restrictions. These limitations play important role when we average the original equation which is not into the standard form, and we can discuss counterexample of it. The following example in order to discourage this hurried averaging:<ref name=":0" />
<math display="block"> \ddot{z} + 4 \varepsilon \cos^2{(t)} \dot{z} + z = 0,  \qquad  z(0) = 0,\quad \dot{z}(0) = 1,
</math>where we put <math>g(z, \dot{z}, t) = - 4\cos^2(t) \dot{z}</math>following the previous notation.

This systems corresponds to a [[damped harmonic oscillator]] where the damping term oscillates between <math>0</math> and <math>4\varepsilon</math>. Averaging the friction term over one cycle of <math>2 \pi</math> yields the equation:
<math display="block">  \ddot{\bar{z}} + 2 \varepsilon \dot{\bar{z}} + \bar{z} = 0, \qquad \bar{z}(0) = 0, \quad  \dot{\bar{z}}(0) = 1.
</math>The solution is
<math display="block">\bar{z}(t) = \frac{1}{(1 - \varepsilon^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}} e^{- \varepsilon t} \sin{((1 - \varepsilon^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}t)}.</math>
which the convergence rate to the origin is <math>\varepsilon</math>. The averaged system obtained from the standard form yields:
<math display="block"> \begin{array}{lcr}
\dot{\bar{r}} = - \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon \bar{r}(2 + \cos(2 \bar{\phi})), ~\bar{r}(0) = 1   \\
\dot{\bar{\phi}} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon \sin(2 \bar{\phi}), ~\bar{\phi}(0) = 0,
\end{array}</math>
which in the rectangular coordinate shows explicitly that indeed the rate of convergence to the origin is <math display="inline">\frac{3}{2} \varepsilon</math> differing from the previous crude averaged system:
<math display="block"> y(t) = e^{-\frac{3}{2} \varepsilon t} \sin{t} </math>

=== Example: Van der Pol Equation ===
[[File:Van der pol qualitative.png|thumb|367x367px|Figure 3: Phase space of a Van der Pol oscillator with <math>\varepsilon = 0.1</math>. The stable limit cycle (orange solid line) in the system is captured correctly by the qualitative analysis of the averaged system. For two different initial conditions ( black dots ) we observe the trajectories.(dashed blue line) converging to the periodic orbit.]]
Van der Pol was concerned with obtaining approximate solutions for equations of the type
<math display="block"> \ddot{z} + \varepsilon (1 - z^2) \dot{z} + z = 0,</math>
where <math>g(z, \dot{z}, t) = (1 - z^2) \dot{z}</math> following the previous notation. This system is often called the [[Van der Pol oscillator]]. Applying periodic averaging to this nonlinear oscillator provides qualitative knowledge of the phase space without solving the system explicitly.

The averaged system is
<math display="block"> \begin{array}{lcr}
\dot{\bar{r}} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon \bar{r}(1 - \frac{1}{4} \bar{r}^2)   \\
\dot{\bar{\phi}} = 0,
\end{array}</math>
and we can analyze the fixed points and their stability. There is an unstable fixed point at the origin and a stable [[limit cycle]] represented by <math>\bar{r} = 2</math>.

The existence of such stable limit-cycle can be stated as a theorem.

'''Theorem (Existence of a periodic orbit)'''<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last1=Guckenheimer|first1=John| last2=Holmes|first2=Philip|series=Applied Mathematical Sciences | date=1983|title=Nonlinear Oscillations, Dynamical Systems, and Bifurcations of Vector Fields| volume=42|language=en-gb|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-1140-2|issn=0066-5452|isbn=978-1-4612-7020-1}}</ref>''':''' If <math>p_0</math>is a hyperbolic fixed point of <br />
<math display="block"> \dot{y}= \varepsilon {\bar {f}}^1(y)</math>Then there exists <math>\varepsilon_0 > 0</math>such that for all <math>0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_0</math>,
<math display="block"> \dot{x} = \varepsilon f^{1}(x, t) + \varepsilon^{2} f^{[2]}(x, t, \varepsilon)</math>
has a unique hyperbolic periodic orbit <math>\gamma_{\varepsilon}(t) = p_0 + \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)</math> of the same stability type as <math>p_0</math>.

The proof can be found at Guckenheimer and Holmes,<ref name=":2" /> Sanders ''et al.'' <ref name=":0" /> and for the angle case in Chicone.<ref name=":1" />

=== Example: Restricting the time interval ===
[[File:Restricting time scale.png|thumb|462x462px|Figure 4: The plot depicts two fundamental quantities the average technique is based on: the bounded and connected region <math>D</math> of the phase space and how long (defined by the constant <math>c</math>)  the averaged solution is valid. For this case, <math display="inline">\ddot{z} + z = 8 \varepsilon \cos{(t)} \dot{z}^2 , ~  z(0) = 0,~ \dot{z}(0) = 1;~ 8 \varepsilon = \frac{2}{15} </math>. Note that both solutions blow up in finite time. &nbsp;Hence, <math>D</math> has been chosen accordingly in order to maintain the boundedness of the solution and the time interval of validity of the approximation is <math>0 \leq \varepsilon t < L < \frac{1}{3}</math>.]]
The average theorem assumes existence of a connected and bounded region <math>D \subset \R^n</math>which affects the time interval <math>L</math> of the result validity. The following example points it out. Consider the
<math display="block"> \ddot{z} + z = 8 \varepsilon \cos{(t)} \dot{z}^2 , ~  z(0) = 0,~ \dot{z}(0) = 1, </math>
where <math>g(z, \dot{z}, t) = 8 \dot{z}^2 \cos(t)</math>.  The averaged system consists of
<math display="block"> \begin{array}{lcr}
\dot{\bar{r}} = 3 \varepsilon \bar{r}^2\cos(\bar{\phi}), ~\bar{r}(0) = 1   \\
\dot{\bar{\phi}} = -\varepsilon \bar{r} \sin(\bar{\phi}), ~\bar{\phi}(0) = 0,
\end{array}</math>
which under this initial condition indicates that the original solution behaves like
<math display="block"> z(t) = \frac{\sin(t)}{1 - 3 \varepsilon t} + \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon), </math>
where it holds on a bounded region over <math>0 \leq \varepsilon t \leq L < \frac{1}{3} </math>.

=== Damped Pendulum ===
Consider a [[pendulum|damped pendulum]] whose point of suspension is vibrated vertically by a small amplitude, high frequency signal (this is usually known as ''[[dithering]]''). The equation of motion for such a pendulum is given by
<math display="block">m(l\ddot{\theta} - ak\omega^2 \sin \omega t \sin \theta) = -mg \sin \theta - k(l\dot{\theta} + a\omega \cos \omega t \sin \theta)</math>
where <math>a \sin \omega t</math> describes the motion of the suspension point, <math>k</math> describes the damping of the pendulum, and <math>\theta</math> is the angle made by the pendulum with the vertical.

The [[phase space]] form of this equation is given by
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot t &= 1 \\
\dot\theta &= p \\
\dot p &= \frac{1}{ml} (mak\omega^2 \sin\omega t \sin \theta - mg\sin\theta - k(l p + a\omega \cos\omega t \sin \theta))
\end{align}</math>
where we have introduced the variable <math>p</math> and written the system as an ''autonomous'', first-order system in <math>(t, \theta, p)</math>-space.

Suppose that the [[angular frequency]] of the vertical vibrations, <math>\omega</math>, is much greater than the natural frequency of the pendulum, <math display="inline">\sqrt{ g/l }</math>. Suppose also that the amplitude of the vertical vibrations, <math>a</math>, is much less than the length <math>l</math> of the pendulum. The pendulum's trajectory in phase space will trace out a [[spiral]] around a curve <math>C</math>, moving along <math>C</math> at the slow rate <math>\sqrt{ g/l }</math> but moving around it at the fast rate <math>\omega</math>. The radius of the spiral around <math>C</math> will be small and proportional to <math>a</math>. The average behaviour of the trajectory, over a timescale much larger than <math>2\pi/\omega</math>, will be to follow the curve <math>C</math>.

== Extension error estimates ==
Average technique for initial value problems has been treated up to now with an validity error estimates of order <math>1/\varepsilon</math>. However, there are circumstances where the estimates can be extended for further times, even the case for all times.<ref name=":0" /> Below we deal with a system containing an asymptotically stable fixed point. Such situation recapitulates what is illustrated in Figure 1.

'''Theorem (Eckhaus''' <ref>{{Cite journal|last=Eckhaus|first=Wiktor|date=1975-03-01|title=New approach to the asymptotic theory of nonlinear oscillations and wave-propagation|journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications|volume=49|issue=3| pages=575–611 |doi=10.1016/0022-247X(75)90200-0|issn=0022-247X|doi-access=free}}</ref>'''/Sanchez-Palencia''' <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sanchez-Palencia|first=Enrique|date=1976-01-01|title=Methode de centrage-estimation de l'erreur et comportement des trajectoires dans l'espace des phases|journal=International Journal of Non-Linear Mechanics|volume=11|issue=4|pages=251–263 |doi=10.1016/0020-7462(76)90004-4|bibcode=1976IJNLM..11..251S|issn=0020-7462}}</ref>''')''' Consider the initial value problem
<math display="block"> \dot{x} = \varepsilon f^{1}(x, t), \qquad x_0 \in D \subseteq \R^n, \quad 0 \leq \varepsilon \ll 1.</math>
Suppose
<math display="block"> \dot{y}= \varepsilon \lim_{T \to \infty}{\frac {1}{T}}\int _{0}^{T}f^1(y, s)~ds =: \varepsilon{\bar {f}}^1(y), \quad y(0, \varepsilon) = x_0</math>
exists and contains an asymptotically stable fixed point <math>y = 0</math> in the linear approximation. Moreover, <math>\bar{f}^1</math>is continuously differentiable with respect to <math>y</math> in <math>D</math> and has a domain of attraction <math>D^0 \subset D</math>. For any compact  <math>K \subset D^0</math> and for all <math>x_0 \in K</math>
<math display="block"> \|x(t) - y(t)\| = \mathcal{O}(\delta(\varepsilon)), \quad 0 \leq t < \infty,</math>
with <math>\delta(\varepsilon) = o(1)</math> in the general case and <math>\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)</math> in the periodic case.
